matters is narrow and solid — among last year's winners, the ones that got there quietly keep going
and the ones that got there in jumps give it back, worth 2.3 points a year and a quarter less churn,
even in large liquid stocks. The finding that does not matter is everything I built on top of it:
swapping the ranking underneath broke it, and nothing about choosing names was ever going to touch a
22% fall caused by a six-week market crash. Do not spend a test-window look on any of these five.
They fail the fall limit on the development window, and four looks have already been spent on books
that failed on the real window for reasons the development window could not see.

Two things next, and I have queued both. First and more interesting: measure smoothness on the
*same* return stream you ranked on — count the up and down days of the market-adjusted move, not the
raw price — inside the residual book. That is a one-line change to a measure that already works, and
this run is good evidence that the mismatch is why the residual version died. If it works it adds
quality to the book you already trade, and the lower churn pays for itself in fees. Second and
duller: the combined book has the best gains-to-losses ratio of any real-fee book in this lab, 2.17,
and the lowest churn, so it is the cheapest book to run a position-size brake on. Your residual book
showed what that brake costs — the lab measured it this week — and it is expensive, roughly a point
and a half of yearly return for every point of fall removed near the limit. Buying 2.8 points of fall
at that rate would cost about four points of return and land near 8%, barely above the market. So I
expect that second one to fail, and I am queuing it anyway, because "expensive" measured once is
worth more than "expensive" assumed forever. The first idea is the one I would spend the next run on.
methods.verdict: Among last year's winners, the ones that climbed quietly beat the ones that jumped by 2.3 points a year (12.1% vs 9.8% on your deposits, 572k vs 436k ended) with a quarter less churn — but every version still fell 22%, over the 20% limit, because a six-week market crash does not care which names you picked.

methods.name: Blend total and residual momentum instead of choosing between them
methods.sourceRef: insight 58's third recommendation; M0007/M0032 (residual) against F4-MOM12 (total)
methods.hypothesis: Insight 58's third recommendation, held back from the 2026-10-09 batch only because the batch had four slots and this was the fifth idea. The lab has treated total momentum and residual momentum as rivals: F4-MOM12-N20-TREND earns +16.2% a year on dev with a 22.2% worst fall, M0007-N20-RAW earns +15.0% with 19.6%, and stripping the market's move out of the ranking was filed as a virtue. Insight 58 complicates that: refusing high-beta names is exactly how a beta-stripped book makes itself a standing bet against a narrow, mega-cap-led market, which is the regime that has run almost unbroken since late 2023. A rank-average of the two scores, or a weight sweep from pure total to pure residual, would say what the lab has never asked: whether the two signals are substitutes or complements, and where on that line the worst fall is smallest per point of return. Run at Gotrade's real fees in fractional shares on the monthly-hold-frac-gotrade preset, funded 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th, so the answer is directly comparable with M0032.

methods.name: Regime gate on the yield curve and credit spreads, not on price
methods.sourceRef: FRED: T10Y2Y, BAA10Y, DGS10, DFII10 (free API)
methods.hypothesis: Every method in this lab shares one risk control: a 200-day SPY trend gate, which is a function of the price it is trying to protect against, and which M0007 own analysis found too slow in Aug 1998. The term spread (T10Y2Y) and the BAA credit spread (BAA10Y) are exogenous, published daily since the 1960s, and turn before equity prices rather than after. Replace or supplement the trend gate with a macro gate: hold the book while credit spreads are not widening and the curve is not inverting, stand down when both deteriorate. Expected failure: macro series are monthly-ish in information even when daily in publication, so the gate fires late in fast shocks (2020) and whipsaws in slow ones; or it simply reproduces the trend gate at a lag, adding a data dependency for nothing.
methods.blockedOn: FRED daily series in the research store: T10Y2Y (term spread), BAA10Y (credit spread), DGS10, DFII10. Free API, no key needed; needs a research_store loader and a manifest file beside fx.csv.

methods.name: Risk gate on the VIX term structure, which turns days before a 200-day average
methods.sourceRef: CBOE VIX and VIX3M daily history, free
methods.hypothesis: The 200-day trend gate needs the market to have already fallen a long way before it reacts; the VIX term structure inverts (VIX above VIX3M) at the start of a shock rather than the middle. Gate the book on that inversion instead. The dev record says exactly where this would pay: M0007 deepest fall was not 2008 or 2000, both of which the trend gate sat out, but the six weeks after June 1998, when the gate had not yet turned off. Expected failure: term-structure inversions are frequent and mostly harmless, so the book is out of the market far more often than the trend gate keeps it out, and the lost compounding costs more than the one fast shock it saves.
methods.blockedOn: CBOE VIX and VIX3M daily closes in the research store. Free; VIX3M history starts 2002-09, so the gate is only testable on the back half of the dev window.

methods.name: Avoid the crowded side of momentum using short interest
methods.sourceRef: FINRA consolidated short interest, published twice monthly, free
methods.hypothesis: Momentum crashes are partly a short-squeeze and crowding phenomenon, and this lab has eleven flavours of momentum and no measure of how crowded any of its picks are. Rank on residual momentum as M0007 does, then drop or underweight the names in the top decile of short interest as a share of float. Expected failure: in a long-only book the crowded names are often simply the best momentum names, so the filter cuts the winners and the return falls more than the drawdown does; or the twice-monthly publication lag makes the measure stale exactly when it would matter.
methods.blockedOn: FINRA consolidated short interest, twice monthly per symbol, plus shares float to make it a ratio. Free download; needs a loader and a point-in-time join on the settlement date, never the publication date.

methods.name: The real-fee residual book behind the fast crash gate, aimed at the summer-of-1998 shock
methods.hypothesis: M0033 proved by elimination that a trailing-volatility brake cannot defend this book: five strengths from TV22 down to TV14 were tested on the real-fee fractional funded configuration, and the worst fall sat at 19.9-20.0% across the three that kept the return, because the binding episode is Jul-Aug 1998 -- fast, and arriving after a calm stretch, so a 21-day volatility estimate reads scale 1.0 on the way in and clamps only during the rebound (skew worsens monotonically from -0.32 unbraked to -0.59 at TV18, the fingerprint of taking none of the fall and some of the recovery). The fall is therefore a timing problem, not a sizing problem, and the lab already owns a tool shaped for it: M0012's fast crash gate, which reads the market's own sudden move over days rather than the basket's trailing jumpiness over a month. This method puts M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT behind that gate instead of under the volatility brake -- same ranking, same screen, same SPY-200 trend gate, same fractional shares at Gotrade's measured fees on the 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up, so the only change from M0032 is the crash gate. I expect it to cut the 20.65% fall to the mid-to-high teens while giving up far less than the brake did, because it acts on the days that actually made the fall rather than taxing every month to pay for days it never catches: the brake charged 1.8 points of yearly return per point of fall removed at the light end, where M0032's unbraked book has the lab's best return per unit of fall at 0.66 and every braked version is worse. The bar to clear is the parent's: beat a deposit-matched SPY's 7.2% a year by a wide margin, keep gains-to-losses near 2.0, and land the worst fall with real room under 20% rather than the three ten-thousandths of a point M0033 cleared it by. 2-4 variants spanning the gate's trigger threshold and its re-entry delay, all fixed before the run.

methods.name: Cut exposure on the account's own fall, not on a forecast of it: the real-fee residual book under a drawdown brake
methods.hypothesis: The companion to M0041, and the opposite philosophy. M0033 showed that forecasting trouble from last month's jumpiness fails on this book because its worst fall (Jul-Aug 1998) begins in calm weather: the brake is off on the way in and on during the rebound, so it worsens the downside lopsidedness from -0.32 to -0.59 while leaving the fall at 19.9%. A drawdown brake makes no forecast at all. It reads the account's own equity against its running peak and cuts exposure once the loss passes a threshold, restoring it as the account recovers -- it responds to the loss rather than predicting it, which is the right shape for a shock nobody can see coming. M0013 already built this machinery for the total-return momentum book (basket_drawdown_brake) and it is the lab's untested answer to exactly this failure mode; the backlog has carried it as M0009 since before the real-fee era. This method applies it to M0032-N20-RAW-FRAC-GT: same ranking, same screen, same trend gate, fractional shares at Gotrade's measured fees on the monthly top-up, so the only change from the parent is the brake. The honest worry, written before the run: a drawdown brake sells after the fall has started and buys back after the recovery has started, which is the textbook way to lock in a loss -- M0019 already showed that protective stops on this family 'fire together in market-wide falls, sell near the bottom and miss the rebound', costing 0.7-2.4 points a year while barely moving the worst fall. So the variants must span the trigger depth (a shallow trigger acts early and whipsaws, a deep one acts too late to help) and the re-entry rule, 3-5 of them fixed in advance. I expect this to beat the volatility brake on the same book -- a lower fall per point of return given up than the brake's 1.8 at the light end -- but I would not be surprised if it, too, cannot beat simply running unbraked, which still holds the lab's best return per unit of fall at 0.66. Either answer settles whether this book's drawdown can be managed at all, or whether it has to be accepted and the method judged on its return.

methods.name: Residual information discreteness: count the up and down days of the residual, not the price
methods.hypothesis: M0036 found the frog-in-the-pan effect alive in this universe on the TOTAL-momentum pool (CONT 12.08% a year money-weighted vs DISC 9.78%, PF 2.09 vs 1.72, turnover 6.42 vs 8.44, 572k vs 436k ended on 149,338 USD paid in) and completely dead on the RESIDUAL pool (RM-CONT 11.90% vs RM-DISC 11.99%, PF 1.85 vs 1.83 -- no separation at all). The obvious explanation, that the residual pool is already continuous so there is nothing left to sort, was MEASURED on 76 quarterly dates 1997-2015 and is false: mean continuity of the top-40 by residual momentum was +0.0516 against +0.0645 for the top-40 by total momentum, with a slightly WIDER within-pool spread (0.0530 vs 0.0490), and the two pools share only 17.7 of 40 names. The remaining explanation is a measurement mismatch: M0036 counted up and down days on each stock's TOTAL daily return while the residual pool is ranked on the market-model RESIDUAL. For a name chosen because its residual drift was steady, the sign pattern of its raw price is dominated by the market's sign pattern, so the count carries no information about the stream the ranking cared about. This method computes information discreteness on the residual daily returns themselves -- sign(cumulative residual) x (share of negative residual days minus share of positive residual days) over the same 12-1 window, from the residuals residual_scores already forms -- and sorts the top-40 residual-momentum pool by it. Frame unchanged from M0032 and M0036: F4's screen, SPY-200 trend gate, top-20, monthly, equal weights, fractional at Gotrade's real fees, funded 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th. Variants: residual-continuous, its registered residual-discrete mirror, and a blended residual-momentum-plus-residual-continuity rank. The mirror is mandatory -- it is the only thing that made M0036's total-momentum result mean anything. I expect the separation to come back at roughly the size it had on the total pool (2 points a year, a quarter less churn) and I expect the worst fall to stay near 20-22% and the method to be rejected on the fall exactly as M0036 was: this buys quality per trade, not safety. If the separation does come back it is a cheap quality gain on the book the owner already trades, and the lower turnover pays for itself at Gotrade's real fees. If it does not come back, the honest conclusion is that the attention effect is absent for residual winners, which closes the family.

methods.name: A brake on the quietest book: the drizzle blend under an own-volatility target
methods.sourceRef: M0036-BLEND (Da, Gurun & Warachka 2014) + M0001's own-volatility overlay (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015) at M0033's targets, on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade
methods.hypothesis: M0036-BLEND has the best gains-to-losses ratio of any real-fee book in the lab (2.17) and the lowest turnover (6.42 against 8.4-9.5 for every other real-fee book), earning 11.95% a year money-weighted against 7.19% for deposit-matched SPY, and it fails one condition only: a 22.28% worst fall against the 20% limit, taken between 17 July and 31 August 1998. Low turnover matters here because a position-size brake works by trading exposure up and down, and at Gotrade's real fees the cheapest book to brake is the one that already trades least. This method puts M0001's own-volatility target over M0036-BLEND's picks, at the same targets M0033 measured on the residual book, and nothing else changes. M0033 priced this exact brake on a sibling: on M0032 it took the fall from 20.65% to 19.98% at a 22% target (costing 1.2 points of annual money-weighted return), to 19.94% at 18% (2.1 points) and to 16.39% at 14% (3.9 points). I therefore EXPECT THIS TO FAIL, and I am registering it so the expectation is measured rather than assumed: buying 2.3 points of fall at roughly a point and a half of return per point of fall would cost about three points and land near 9% a year, still above the deposit-matched market but well below the 13.68% of the book the owner already has, and the luck score would likely drop below the 0.90 bar as the daily Sharpe falls. The one way it surprises me is if the drizzle book's falls are concentrated in weeks where the BOOK itself was visibly jumpy beforehand -- 1998 and 2011 were both preceded by rising volatility, unlike the calm pre-fall markets that defeated M0002 -- in which case the brake catches more of the fall per point of return than it did on the residual book. Variants: own-vol targets of 22%, 18% and 14% on a 21-session reading, plus one no-brake control re-stating BLEND under the same allocator so the comparison is within-run; the control should reproduce M0036-BLEND's numbers exactly.
methods.expectedFailure: The 1998 fall arrived faster than a one-month volatility reading can follow, so the light 22% target sits at full exposure through it and buys almost nothing, the 18% target buys about a point of fall and stays above 20%, and only the 14% target clears the limit -- at a cost of three to four points of yearly return and a luck score under 0.90. A second way it fails: a calm, continuous-momentum basket has low own volatility most of the time, so the brake binds rarely and then all at once, and the monthly resize trades it places at the bottom of a fall lock in losses that the unbraked book would have recovered; the braked variants then lose return without a matching fall cut.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

The drizzle blend (M0036-BLEND) picks 20 stocks whose past year's rise came in many small steady days, not a few big jumps. It earned your money 11.95% a year against 7.19% for the same deposits put into SPY, and it failed one rule only: its worst fall was 22.28%, over the 20% limit. That fall happened in the summer of 1998.

This method kept those exact picks and added a brake. Each month it measures how jumpy the 20-stock basket was over the last 21 trading days. If the basket was jumpier than a target, it buys less and holds the rest in cash. There were three targets (22%, 18% and 14% yearly volatility), plus a control with no brake. Everything ran at Gotrade's real fees, in fractional shares, with 5,000,000 IDR added on the 25th of each month.

## Results (dev window 1996 to 2015, money-weighted, same deposits into SPY earned +7.2% a year)

| variant | your money a year | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck score (DSR) | time invested | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no brake (control) | +12.0% | 22.3% | 2.17 | 0.930 | 70% | fails: fall over 20% |
| 22% target | +11.1% | 22.0% | 2.14 | 0.925 | 67% | fails: fall over 20% |
| 18% target | +10.2% | 21.9% | 2.08 | 0.907 | 64% | fails: fall over 20% |
| **14% target** | **+8.7%** | **19.2%** | 2.07 | **0.901** | 56% | **passes all five conditions** |

- The control matches M0036-BLEND number for number (22.28% fall, 2.17, 1,199 trades), so the brake code changed nothing except the brake.
- **Luck score.** N is 34 (one look per distinct method, as `lab status` prints it). At that N, TV14's 0.901 says there is about a 90% chance the edge is real and not the best of 34 lucky tries. That is just over the 0.90 bar, by one thousandth.
- **Worst year.** 2008, at -0.1%. The market-trend switch had the book in cash for most of that crash. The worst *fall* was the fast 1998 shock.
- The trade count stayed at 1,199 for every variant. A brake on a monthly book only resizes positions; it does not add round trips. Turnover even fell, from 6.42 to 6.04.

## Why it worked the way it did

1998 was a fast fall. A one-month jumpiness reading only rises once the fall has already started, so the light brakes were still near full size when it hit. The 22% target took 0.27 points off the worst fall and cost 0.9 points a year. The 18% target took 0.36 points off and cost 1.8. Those two paid for a brake that never caught the fall. Only the 14% target holds the book small often enough to be partly in cash *before* a shock: 56% invested against 70%. It took 3.1 points off the fall and cost 3.25 points a year, about one point of return per point of fall. That is roughly the price M0033 paid on the residual book (0.9). The drizzle book is not cheaper to brake, despite its low turnover.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **The hypothesis's main forecast held almost exactly:** "land near 9% a year" (actual 8.7%), with only the hardest brake clearing the limit. The surprise it allowed for, that this book is cheaper to brake because its jumpiness warns ahead of a fall, **did not happen**.
- **Expected failure #1 happened** as written: the light targets bought almost nothing, and only the 14% target cleared the limit, at a cost of over three points a year. The forecast was a luck score under 0.90. It came in at 0.901, a hair above.
- Expected failure #2 (the brake selling at the bottom) cannot be seen in the totals.

## The durability check, which is the real finding

`lab status` lists M0044 as promotable. The method-level fold record is 3 of 4 folds beaten, and no relative has failed a test. But that 3-of-4 belongs to the walk-forward's *selection rule*, which picked the no-brake or light variants in most folds. **The variant that would actually be promoted (TV14, the only eligible one) beats SPY in just 1 of the 4 walk-forward folds.** By fold, in points a year against SPY: 2003-05 -1.2, 2006-08 +9.1, 2009-11 -11.8, 2012-14 -3.0.

By era, TV14's edge over SPY is +1.4 points a year in 1996-2001, +8.6 in 2002-2008 and **-7.1 in 2009-2015**. 2009-2015 is when the data covers the most companies, and the walk-forward prints -5.2 for the method. The whole edge is the 2002-2008 bear market, when the trend switch had the book in cash. In the years that look most like the market since 2016, the braked book lost to SPY by seven points a year. The parent has the same shape: BLEND is -4.8 in 2009-2015. The brake makes it worse, because a cash-heavy book falls further behind in a steady bull market.

The buy-data signal does not fire: condition (d), a positive 2009-2015 edge, fails.

## My opinion:

Do not spend a test-window look on M0044-TV14, even though the hard gate would let it through. Four of four test looks have already failed on "beats SPY", and this candidate shows the exact pattern behind those failures. It wins only in the 2002-2008 crash era. It loses to SPY by seven points a year in the best-covered recent era. It beats SPY in one of four folds as a fixed configuration. It clears the luck bar by 0.001. Spending the look would almost certainly buy a fifth `test-failed`, and that would also block the whole stock-momentum-attention family (the drizzle idea) by kinship. An own-volatility brake on a monthly book is a priced-out direction: two books, two prices, both about a point of return per point of fall. The lab should stop trying it. What deserves the next trial is the drizzle signal's weakness after 2009, not its 1998 fall. It is a stock picker that needs the 2002-2008 cash period to win. The next idea tests that directly: hold the drizzle picks *without* the trend switch's cash periods, with SPY as the parking spot instead of cash, and see whether the stock picking alone beats SPY from 2009 on.


### 2026-10-09

### 2026-10-09 -- Sera 20261009-2105: no look spent

The hard gate would take this method (3 of 4 folds at the method level, no kin has test-failed), so declining is Sera's judgement, not a refusal. Promotion would pre-register the only eligible variant, the 14% brake. That configuration on its own wins 1 of 4 walk-forward folds; the method-level 3 of 4 comes from the lighter brakes, which the fold rule picks and which all fail the fall limit. It clears the 20% fall limit by 0.8 points and the luck bar by 0.001. In 2009-2015, the best-covered stretch and the one most like the years the look would score, the method's pick trails SPY by 5.2 points a year (the 14% brake by about 7). Every one of the four looks spent so far failed on beating SPY, and the evidence here points the same way. A fifth failed look would also close this family, the drizzle signal, which is the one stock-picking idea the last batch called genuinely new, along with its queued follow-ups. The look is kept for a configuration whose own fold record and recent-era edge support it.
methods.verdict: Only the hardest brake gets the drizzle book under the 20% fall limit (+8.7% a year vs SPY's +7.2%, luck score 0.901), but it loses to SPY by 7 points a year after 2009; do not spend a test look on it

methods.name: De-crowding weights under the own-volatility brake: two small fixes against the last half point of fall
methods.hypothesis: M0034 turned the weight dial in both directions and found the only improvement on the side nobody asked about: weights proportional to one over the square root of 20-day mean dollar volume beat the equal-weight control on every axis at once -- money-weighted +14.0% a year vs +13.7%, max DD 20.62% vs 20.65%, Sharpe 0.891 vs 0.849, MAR 0.679 vs 0.663, DSR 0.962 vs 0.944 at N=32 -- at 5% more turnover and with no name ever above 12.5% of the book (effective names 17.0 of 20, against 8.6 for the size-proportional tilt). The mechanism is that dollar volume inside a top-20 momentum book is an attention measure, not a size measure, so leaning away from it is a systematic underweight of the most crowded trade; M0034-SIZE proved the point from the other end by putting 61% in QCOM on 1999-12-31 and taking a 28.8% fall through the dot-com break. Three tenths of a point a year is not enough on its own and M0034-INV-SQRT still failed max DD <= 20% by six tenths of a point, exactly as its parent M0032 did. This method combines it with the own-volatility brake already queued for this family (M0033), which attacks the drawdown directly rather than incidentally: same ranking, same screen, same SPY-200 gate, same fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up, with the de-crowding weights underneath the brake instead of equal weights. The two fixes are close to independent -- the brake scales total exposure through time, the weights redistribute within the book at a point in time -- so if the brake alone lands near 19-20% as M0033 hopes, the de-crowding weights should be worth the last fraction without costing the return the brake already pays for. Run the brake at two or three settings against a de-crowded control so the interaction is readable, and do not promote a variant whose improvement comes only from the brake: the point is whether the pair closes the half point, not whether either does.

methods.name: Crowding as a rank penalty, not a weight: punish momentum earned on abnormal volume
methods.hypothesis: M0034 found that the LEVEL of 20-day mean dollar volume behaves like a crowding measure inside a top-20 momentum book -- weighting by it put 61% in QCOM on 1999-12-31, 59% in CSCO+QCOM at the March 2000 top and 75% in AAPL+META in June 2014, and took a 28.8% max DD; weighting away from it beat the equal-weight control on every axis (MAR 0.679 vs 0.663, Sharpe 0.891 vs 0.849, DSR 0.962 vs 0.944 at N=32). But the LEVEL is a confounded measure: it mixes how big a company is with how excited the market currently is about it, and the lab measured those two apart only weakly (Spearman 0.686 against point-in-time market value over 2010-2015). The clean crowding measure is the CHANGE, not the level: a name's 20-day mean dollar volume divided by its own trailing one-year mean, which cancels the size component entirely because each name is compared only to itself. A ratio near 1 is a stock trading normally; a ratio of 3 is a stock the crowd has just arrived at. This method keeps M0032's execution exactly -- fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, the 5,000,000 IDR monthly top-up, the SPY-200 gate, monthly, top 20 -- and puts the crowding ratio into the RANKING rather than the weighting: subtract a multiple of the cross-sectional z-score of log relative volume from the residual-momentum score, so that between two names with the same momentum the one that earned it quietly is preferred. This is the same instinct as the frog-in-the-pan idea already queued (M0036), which prefers momentum earned in a drizzle over momentum earned in jumps, but read off volume rather than off the shape of the returns, and the two should be run close together so the lab learns which reading of 'quiet' is the one that pays. Vary the penalty multiple over 3-4 settings plus an unpenalised control. Expected failure: relative volume spikes on earnings for every name regardless of crowding, so the penalty mostly fires on the earnings calendar and ranks by reporting date; or the penalty removes exactly the names momentum needs, since a stock the crowd is arriving at is also a stock that keeps rising, and the 1999 lesson is survivorship in reverse -- the crowding that killed the size tilt in 2000 is the same crowding that paid it +15.0% a year overall.

methods.name: The real market-value tilt, once the lab can say how big a company was before 2009
methods.hypothesis: The question the reserved M0034 idea actually asked is still unanswered. M0034 tested a tilt by 20-day mean dollar volume because that is the only size measure the store carries back to 1993; EDGAR's XBRL facts begin in 2009 and the dev window opens in 1996, so a book requiring a filed share count would hold nothing for thirteen of twenty years. Measured over the 2010-2015 overlap, trading size and market value rank the eligible set alike at Spearman 0.686 and put 35-40% of the money on different names, so M0034's verdict is about crowding and not about company size. Two things must land before this can be run honestly. First, a point-in-time shares-outstanding series back to the mid-1990s (see the data-wish journal entry): commercial and academic datasets carry it, and a quarterly figure dated by when it became public is enough. Second, the lab's market-value figure must stop multiplying an unadjusted share count by a split-adjusted close -- today that reads Apple at 20 billion dollars on 2014-06-30 against a real 560 billion, correct for names that never split again and wrong by a factor of 28 for names that did, which is look-ahead-shaped because the error depends on splits after the data date. One caution already measured and worth pre-registering: a TRUE cap weighting of this top-20 book over 2010-2015 would have been MORE concentrated than the volume tilt, not less -- a mean 36% in one name and effectively under seven names -- so this idea should be written with a ceiling from the start, and its real question is not 'does cap weighting beat equal weighting' but 'is there any ceiling at which a size tilt earns its concentration'.
methods.blockedOn: point-in-time shares outstanding before 2009 (EDGAR XBRL starts 2009; the dev window opens 1996), and a market-value figure that does not multiply an unadjusted share count by a split-adjusted close

methods.name: Trim toward the market when the book is furthest AHEAD of it, not when it is behind
methods.hypothesis: M0035 measured the exact opposite of what it hoped and the measurement is the gift: the binding dev fall (9 May - 21 Jul 2006, -20.7%) happened while the book was AHEAD of SPY by 11.8 points over the trailing twelve months, and still ahead by 6.0 points a month in. The relative-shortfall switch was off through the whole fall, by its own rule, and turned on ten days after the bottom. The same pattern sits under the lab's other binding falls: a momentum book owns whatever has already run furthest, so its worst falls arrive immediately after its best relative runs, not after its worst. M0027 proposes to read the top-minus-bottom decile spread for the same 2006 fall and warns it may turn only after the damage; this reads a slower, simpler quantity that is high BEFORE the damage rather than after it. Keep M0032 verbatim -- top-20 raw cumulative residual momentum, F4's screen, the SPY-200 trend gate, monthly, equal weights, fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees, 5,000,000 IDR on the 25th -- and reuse M0035's shadow-book machinery unchanged, only inverting the comparison: when the book's trailing twelve-month return is AHEAD of SPY's by more than a threshold, trim the stock book to a fraction of the account and hold the rest in SPY, releasing as the lead narrows. Variants sweep the threshold (ahead by 10, 15 and 20 points) and the trim (hold three quarters, hold half), against the same unbraked control. This is the only go-live condition the whole residual-momentum family still fails: M0032 and all six M0035 variants miss max DD <= 20% by about six tenths of a point and nothing else. If trimming after a big relative run takes 20.6% below 20% while costing less than the roughly one point a year it would have to cost to still beat a deposit-matched SPY by five points, the family finally has a dev-eligible member at real fees. Expected failure: the lead is a near-permanent state for a book that beat SPY by seven points a year on dev, so an ahead-by-10 trigger is on most of the time and simply becomes a permanent half-SPY core wearing a disguise -- in which case M0030's always-on core is the honest version of it and this adds nothing but a dial. The second failure is that trimming a winner is the classic way to cap the upside without capping the fall, since the 2006 drop took three months from a peak the trim would have been on for, but at only a quarter to a half of the book the fall is reduced by a quarter to a half of six tenths of a point -- not enough.

methods.name: The market-core-plus-momentum book at Gotrade's real fees: the twin its promotion needs
methods.hypothesis: M0035 and its two siblings agree that the lab's 20% worst-fall wall only moves when the book holds less ALL the time rather than less sometimes: five different pickers spanned six tenths of a point of fall (M0036), six conditional relative-shortfall settings moved it not at all (M0035, every variant at 20.6%), and the only thing that reached a 16.4% fall was a permanent own-volatility cut that gave up about two points of yearly return (M0033-TV14-N21). M0030-C50T is the lab's other permanent holder-of-less: half SPY, half the residual-momentum book, 12.7% a year on dev at an 18.6% worst fall, under the limit, and it is dev-eligible today. But it ran on monthly-hold-frac at the old flat 0.1% a trade, so its numbers cannot be compared with the real-fee ones and, under the promotion rule in force since M0031, it cannot be promoted as it stands: a method from M0030 or earlier needs lab costs run on it first, and then its best variant re-registered as a one-variant variation on the -gotrade preset and re-run on dev before a test-window look may be spent. This idea is that twin. One variant, M0030-C50T's configuration verbatim -- BLEND of the timed SPY core at 50% with RESIDMOM on M0011's RAW20 params at 50% -- on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the owner's monthly top-up, so the look is spent on the configuration paper would actually trade. The hypothesis is that it survives: the blend turns over about the same 1,615 times as M0032, roughly 80 trades a year, which is slow enough that a fee schedule with a ten-cent floor cannot eat the margin, and M0032 already showed this exact fee change costing a point and a half a year while leaving every condition it cleared still cleared. Expected failure: the SPY core halves the stock book's slot sizes, so each stock order is a -35 slice where the ten-cent floor is half a percent a side rather than a quarter, and the fee drag lands well above M0032's 15.6% of gross trade profit -- pushing the money-weighted return under the deposit-matched SPY even though the lump-sum version beat it, which is the one way a core-plus-satellite book can fail a funded comparison that its unfunded parent passed.

methods.name: Momentum earned overnight only: rank on the gaps between yesterday's close and today's open
methods.sourceRef: Lou, Polk & Skouras (2019), A tug of war: overnight versus intraday expected returns, Journal of Financial Economics 134(1), 192-213, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.03.011
methods.hypothesis: Lou, Polk and Skouras find that essentially all of momentum's abnormal return is earned overnight (close to next open), while the intraday part (open to close) of the same stocks runs the other way, because individuals push prices overnight and institutions trade against the characteristic during the day; the split is strongest in large, high-price stocks, which is F4's universe. The lab has ranked on twelve-month total and residual return eleven ways and never separated WHEN the return was earned. Each month, among F4's screened members, rank on the sum of the last twelve months' (skip the latest month) overnight log returns and hold the top 20 equal weight behind the SPY 200-day gate, in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the owner's funding. Variants: ON (overnight rank), ID (intraday rank, the control the paper says should lose), TOT (plain 12-1 total momentum in the same run, the yardstick), TUG (overnight rank minus intraday rank, the paper's tug-of-war spread as a long-only pick) and TOT-ON (the 40 best total-momentum names, then the 20 of them whose gain came most overnight). Success: ON or TOT-ON beats TOT on return per unit of worst fall and ID is the worst of the set. Assumption: the store's prices are split-adjusted, not dividend-adjusted, and an allocator cannot see dividends, so the ex-dividend gap stays inside the overnight leg; this tilts ON slightly away from high-yield names and is not corrected.
methods.expectedFailure: Daily open prices before about 2001 are noisy (fractional ticks, opens recorded equal to the prior close on thin days) and split adjustment can leave rounding in the open, so the overnight sum carries measurement noise the close-to-close sum does not. Overnight returns are small and the twelve-month sum is dominated by a handful of earnings-announcement gaps, so ON may simply be an earnings-surprise momentum book with the same 20%-plus fall in 1998 and 2008 as every other momentum book. Worse, ranking on the overnight leg alone rewards names with large gap risk -- high-volatility, high-news stocks -- so ON's worst fall may be larger than TOT's, not smaller. The intraday control may not lose either: in a large-cap universe the intraday leg is the institutional leg and may carry the low-volatility tilt that has helped every blend in this lab.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

A stock's daily move has two parts. The **overnight** part is the jump from yesterday's close to today's open. The **daytime** part is the move from the open to the close. A 2019 study (Lou, Polk and Skouras) found that nearly all of momentum's extra return comes overnight. The daytime part of the same stocks tends to go the other way. This method tests that on our stocks. Each month it ranks the stocks by the last year's overnight jumps only, skipping the latest month, and holds the top 20.

Everything else stays the same as the lab's standard momentum book: the same 539 large stocks and liquidity screen, all cash when SPY is below its 200-day average, 20 names in equal amounts, fractional shares, Gotrade's real fees, and your funding plan (10M IDR to start, then 5M IDR on the 25th of each month). The five versions:

- **ON**: the 20 stocks with the biggest overnight gains.
- **ID**: the 20 stocks with the biggest daytime gains. This is the control. The study says it should do worst.
- **TOT**: plain 12-month momentum, run in the same test as the yardstick.
- **TUG**: overnight rank minus daytime rank, the study's "tug of war" spread, buying only.
- **TOT-ON**: the 40 best plain-momentum stocks, then the 20 of them whose gain came most overnight.

## Results (dev window 1996 → Oct 2015, your deposits)

| version | your money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ON | **16.9%** | 7.2% | 30.5% | 2.83 | 0.973 |
| TOT-ON | **15.1%** | 7.2% | 22.8% | 2.41 | 0.956 |
| TOT (yardstick) | 13.8% | 7.2% | 23.3% | 2.05 | 0.940 |
| TUG | 12.0% | 7.2% | 35.8% | 1.98 | 0.890 |
| ID (control) | 8.1% | 7.2% | 27.7% | 1.67 | 0.720 |

ON and TOT-ON are the two highest returns on your deposits the lab has recorded at real fees. The next best is the size-tilted residual book at 15.0%, which fell 28.8% at its worst. The real-fee residual book (the lab's reference) earned 13.7% with a 20.6% worst fall.

**Every version fails the same rule: the worst fall must be no more than 20%.** TOT-ON misses by 2.8 points and ON by 10.5 points. Every other rule passes for ON, TOT-ON and TOT: they beat SPY, gains outweigh losses by far more than 1.3×, and they make over 100 trades.

**Luck test.** The DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at N = 36, the lab's count of independent tries, against the bar of 0.90. ON (0.973), TOT-ON (0.956) and TOT (0.940) clear it. TUG (0.890) and ID (0.720) do not.

## When it hurt

- **ON**'s worst fall ran from spring 2011 to spring 2012: the August 2011 debt-ceiling selloff, then a weak May 2012. The overnight ranking had loaded up on names that gap on news, and those fell hardest when the market fell. Its worst calendar year is 2011 (−6.9%).
- **TOT-ON**'s worst fall is the summer of 1998, the Russia/LTCM shock, when every momentum book in this lab falls. The SPY 200-day gate turns off only after the damage. Its worst calendar year is only 2015 (−1.8%).
- **TOT**'s worst fall was in mid-2006.
- 2001–2003 and 2008–mid-2009 are flat on every curve: the trend gate held cash. On average about 70% of the money was invested.

## Why

The study's split shows up clearly here. Ranking on the overnight part alone beat ranking on the whole return by 3.1 points a year. Ranking on the daytime part alone barely beat SPY (8.1% vs 7.2%). So the daytime half of momentum carries almost none of its reward in this universe either. The control lost, as the study predicts. That is the strongest evidence that the effect is real and not a fluke of the window.

The cost is in the falls. Overnight jumps cluster in stocks that make news: earnings surprises, upgrades, deals. A book full of those stocks moves together when the market panics, so ON's worst fall is the biggest of the safe-looking versions. TOT-ON keeps the plain-momentum filter first. That holds onto the steadier winners and uses the overnight measure only to choose among them. It keeps most of the return gain (+1.3 points over TOT), and its worst fall is a little smaller than TOT's (22.8% vs 23.3%). Its gains-vs-losses ratio is much better (2.41 vs 2.05).

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis: held.** ON and TOT-ON both beat TOT on return per unit of worst fall (MAR, return divided by worst fall: TOT-ON 0.66 vs TOT 0.59). ID was the worst of the set.
- **Expected failure: partly happened.** I predicted ON would carry the same 20%-plus falls as every momentum book, possibly larger because it favours stocks that gap. That is exactly what happened to ON (30.5%), and TUG was worse still (35.8%). The worry about noisy pre-2001 opens did not show up as a weak result: ON's edge holds across the window.
- **Assumption kept:** dividends are not visible to the ranking, so the price drop on each ex-dividend morning counts as an overnight loss. That tilts ON a little away from high-dividend stocks. A version with dividends added back may score differently.

## Other checks (report only; no trial recorded)

- **Walk-forward:** 3 of 4 out-of-sample folds beaten, with a +1.1% edge in 2009–2015, the years when the store's coverage is best. The walk-forward shows "not dev-eligible" only because nothing in this method cleared the 20% fall limit.
- **Narrow vs broad markets:** ON pays in both (+6.9% / +11.7% vs SPY). TOT-ON's edge is mostly in narrow months (+16.0% vs +3.4%).
- No version is dev-eligible, so nothing was promoted and no test-window look was spent.

## My opinion:

This is the most interesting new signal the lab has found in a while, and it is worth more trials. The control lost as the study predicts, the overnight versions top the lab's funded returns, and the edge survives into 2009–2015. TOT-ON is the version to build on. It failed only the fall limit, by under 3 points, and the fall is the familiar summer-1998 shock, not something new. Next I would put TOT-ON's selection under the lab's existing tools that shrink falls without changing the picks: an own-volatility brake read weekly (which cut the residual book's fall from 14.1% to 12.4%), or a wider 30-name book. I would also try the overnight split on the residual ranking, the lab's best ranking key. One caution: the overnight family is new, so no test-window failure counts against it yet. That makes it one of the few lines that could still reach a counted look.
methods.verdict: Momentum earned overnight is the real thing: picking last year's winners by their overnight jumps earned your money 15.1-16.9% a year vs 7.2% in SPY, the lab's best funded results, while the daytime-only control barely beat SPY - but every version still fell more than 20% at its worst (22.8% at best, in the 1998 shock).

methods.name: Buy the stocks about to pay their dividend: the dividend-month premium
methods.sourceRef: Hartzmark & Solomon (2013), The dividend month premium, J. Financial Economics 109(3), 640-660, doi:10.1016/j.jfineco.2013.02.015
methods.hypothesis: Hartzmark-Solomon find stocks earn about 0.4-0.5 points a month more in months when they are predicted to pay a dividend (they paid one in the same calendar month a year, or a quarter, earlier), with returns rising into the ex-date and turning negative after it, consistent with price pressure from investors who want dividends; the premium is as large as the value premium and less volatile, and it is predicted from the dividend history alone, which the store holds. This is a calendar mechanism the lab has never tried: it reads neither past price level nor volatility, so its picks should be largely unrelated to the momentum books whose correlated crashes set every worst fall so far. Each month, among F4's screened members, find the stocks predicted to go ex-dividend this month (an ex-date in the same calendar month 12 months ago, and for quarterly payers 3 months ago, using only ex-dates known before the rebalance), and hold them equal weight for the month; variants: ALL predicted payers, TOP20 by trailing twelve-month dividend yield among them, TOP20 by lowest 60-day volatility among them, and each of ALL behind and without the SPY 200-day gate. It runs in fractional shares at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's real funding (a -frac-gotrade preset, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, 10M IDR start plus 5M on the 25th) -- fractional is essential because the ALL book holds dozens of names. Success: beats SPY TR money-weighted with a worst fall under 20% and a monthly correlation with the residual-momentum book well under 0.5. Expected failure: a quarter of large caps pay in any given month so the ALL book is close to an equal-weight dividend-payer index, near-total monthly turnover at Gotrade's fees and the 30% US dividend withholding on the owner's account eat most of a half-point monthly premium, and in 2008 dividend payers fell with the market so the ungated book falls 40%+.
methods.blockedOn: dividend ex-date calendar handed to the allocator: the research store holds every cash dividend (dividends.csv, split-adjusted), but Market carries only bars, membership, FX and fundamentals, so prepare/prepare_market never see an ex-date; the dividends reach only the book engine's cash ledger. Needs Market.dividends (point-in-time: an ex-date is usable once it is dated <= data_date) threaded from research.load_store into Market, a test-window equivalent, and a purity test. Bars are split- but not dividend-adjusted, and a ~0.5% ex-date gap cannot be told from daily noise, so there is no price-only proxy.

methods.name: Hold the stock book only over the turn of the month, SPY the rest of the time
methods.sourceRef: Lakonishok & Smidt (1988), Are seasonal anomalies real? A ninety-year perspective, Rev. Financial Studies 1(4); McConnell & Xu (2008), Equity returns at the turn of the month, Financial Analysts Journal 64(2)
methods.hypothesis: McConnell and Xu find that across 1926-2005 essentially all of the US equity premium arrived in the four sessions from the last trading day of a month through the third of the next, as month-end pay and pension flows are invested; the rest of the month earned about the risk-free rate. The dividend-month premium (M0051) is blocked on plumbing, but this calendar mechanism reads only the calendar, which every allocator already has. Test it as a tilt, not a timing switch, so it cannot lose the equity premium by sitting in cash: hold SPY all month, and over the turn-of-month window swap a slice (25, 50, 100%) of it into the highest-beta quarter of F4's screened members (60-day beta to SPY), equal weight, fractional, at Gotrade's real fees on the owner's funding. Success: beats SPY TR money-weighted with a worst fall under 20%. Expected failure: two round trips a month on the slice at Gotrade's fees (about 0.5% per small order) cost more than the extra beta earns over four days, and the effect has faded since its publication, so the dev window's second half (2004-2015) shows nothing.

methods.name: Overnight-picked winners under a weekly volatility brake: the 1998 fall is the only thing left to fix
methods.sourceRef: M0050-TOT-ON (Lou, Polk & Skouras 2019) + M0022's weekly own-volatility brake (Barroso & Santa-Clara 2015), on monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade, funded monthly
methods.hypothesis: M0050-TOT-ON (the 40 best 12-1 momentum names, then the 20 whose gain came most overnight) earned 15.1% a year on the owner's deposits at real fees against 7.2% for deposit-matched SPY, DSR 0.956 at N=36, gains-to-losses 2.41, and failed one condition only: a 22.8% worst fall in the summer-1998 shock. That shock started inside a month, which is exactly the case a weekly re-read of the basket's own volatility was built for: on the residual book the weekly brake cut the worst fall from 14.1% to 12.4% at the same target. Keep TOT-ON's selection exactly, choose the basket monthly, and every week scale it by min(1, target / its own one-month volatility), on monthly-rank-weekly-resize-frac-gotrade with the owner's funding. Variants: targets of 14%, 16% and 18% a year on the 20-name book; a 30-name book (pool 60) at 16%, which should be steadier and so brake less; and the overnight sort run inside the residual-momentum pool (M0007-N20-RAW's ranking, the real-fee residual book's) at 16%. I expect TOTON20-TV18 to be the best trade-off: the overnight book runs hotter than the residual book (it carries news-gap stocks), so an 18% target binds in shocks without clamping calm years, and should land near an 18-19% fall while keeping about 13.5-14% a year funded. Success: at least one version under the 20% fall limit with a funded return above the real-fee residual book's 13.7%. The residual-pool version should have the shallowest fall, because residual ranking strips out market beta before the overnight sort adds news exposure back.
methods.expectedFailure: Every brake in this lab has cost about one point of yearly return per point of fall it saved (insight on M0044). Buying 2.8 points of fall at that rate leaves about 12% a year, under the residual book's 13.7%, so the success bar fails even if the fall bar passes. Worse, weekly resizing at Gotrade's real fees places many small orders on a 20-30 name book funded 5M IDR a month: each resize pays the 0.10 USD floor on slices worth tens of dollars, which can eat the overnight edge's 1.3-point lead over plain momentum. The 1998 fall was fast (mid-July to end of August): a one-month volatility reading may still be low at the first weekly check after the drop starts, so the light 18% target buys little. The 30-name version may dilute the overnight sort into plain momentum and lose the edge. The residual pool may conflict with the overnight sort: residual winners are the steady, low-gap names, so the overnight leg among them may be mostly dividend noise.
methods.analysis:
### 2026-10-09

## What was tried

M0050's best version (TOT-ON) picks the 40 strongest stocks of the past year, then keeps the 20 whose gain came mostly **overnight** (the jump from one day's close to the next day's open). On your deposits it earned 15.1% a year against 7.2% for the same deposits in SPY. It failed one rule only: it fell 22.8% at its worst, in the summer-1998 shock. The limit is 20%.

This method keeps exactly the same picks and adds the lab's **weekly volatility brake**. The basket is still chosen once a month. Every week, the brake checks how much the 20 stocks together swung over the last month. If they swung more than a set target, it sells part of every holding and parks the money in cash. Everything runs in fractional shares, at Gotrade's real fees, with your funding plan (10M IDR to start, then 5M IDR a month).

Five versions, all fixed before any result:
- **TOTON20-TV14 / TV16 / TV18**: the 20-name book with the brake set to 14%, 16% and 18% a year.
- **TOTON30-TV16**: 30 names chosen from the 60 strongest, at 16%.
- **RESON20-TV16**: the overnight sort run inside the residual-momentum pool (the lab's real-fee reference book's ranking), at 16%.

## Results (dev window 1996 → Oct 2015, your deposits, real fees)

| version | your money earned a year | same deposits in SPY | worst fall | gains vs losses | luck test (DSR) | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| no brake (M0050-TOT-ON, parent) | 15.1% | 7.2% | 22.8% | 2.41 | 0.956 | failed fall |
| TOTON20-TV18 | 11.1% | 7.2% | 21.0% | 2.13 | 0.931 | failed fall |
| TOTON20-TV16 | 10.5% | 7.2% | 18.8% | 2.16 | 0.931 | passes |
| TOTON30-TV16 | 10.6% | 7.2% | 19.0% | 2.27 | **0.949** | passes |
| RESON20-TV16 | 10.2% | 7.2% | 17.5% | 1.83 | 0.934 | passes |
| TOTON20-TV14 | 9.3% | 7.2% | 16.3% | 2.12 | 0.917 | passes |

Four of five versions pass every go-live rule on the dev window, so the method is marked dev-eligible. They all beat SPY, all fell less than 20%, gains outweighed losses by far more than the 1.3× required, and all traded more than 100 times.

**The luck test.** DSR asks how likely a result is real rather than the best of many tries. It was judged at N = 37, the lab's count of independent methods, against the bar of 0.90. All five clear it. The 30-name version clears it best (0.949).

**But the success bar I set failed, badly.** I asked for a version under the 20% fall limit that still earned more than the 13.7% a year of the real-fee residual-momentum book (M0032). The best passing version earned 10.6%. It even trails the residual book's own braked twin (M0033-TV22, 12.5% a year with a 20.0% fall).

**Worst years.** Every version's worst calendar year is 2011, and a mild one: −2.8% to −5.4%.

## The price of the brake

The brake took 4.0 points off the worst fall (22.8% → 18.8% at 16%). It cost 4.6 points of yearly return (15.1% → 10.5%). That is worse than the roughly one point of return per point of fall that every other brake in this lab has cost. The 18% target bought only 1.8 points of fall and still cost 4.0 points of return.

**Why so expensive here?** The overnight book picks stocks that jump on news: earnings surprises, upgrades, deals. Those stocks are jumpy all the time, not just in crashes. So a volatility brake reads this book as "too risky" in ordinary months too, and keeps it partly in cash while it is quietly making money. The brake cannot tell good jumpiness (news gaps that keep going up) from bad jumpiness (a market panic). On the calmer residual book, the brake only clamps in real shocks, which is why it was cheap there.

The fee worry did not come true in the way I feared. The trade count stayed at 1,100 for every 20-name version, exactly the parent's count. The cost came from sitting in cash, not from fees.

## Durability checks (report only, nothing recorded)

- **Walk-forward folds: 2 of 4.** The lab re-ran the choice four times, each time picking a version using only the years before, then scoring it on years it had never seen. It beat SPY in only two of the four. The lab's hard gate needs a clear majority, so `lab promote` would refuse this method.
- **2009–2015, the years with the most complete data: −3.8% a year against SPY.** The edge lives in the earlier years. That is the pattern that warned of the four methods that later failed out of sample.
- **Market breadth:** pays in both narrow and broad markets, except the hardest brake (TV14), which pays only when a few big names carry the index. As the lab has learned, this test rarely separates good from bad methods.

So no buy signal: it misses (c) the folds and (d) the 2009–2015 edge.

## Hypothesis and expected failure

- **Hypothesis: failed.** I expected TV18 to land near an 18–19% fall at 13.5–14% a year. It landed at a 21.0% fall and 11.1%. I expected the residual-pool version to have the shallowest fall at the same target. It did (17.5%), but with the weakest gains vs losses (1.83).
- **Expected failure: happened, and worse than written.** I wrote that the brake would cost about a point per point of fall and leave about 12% a year. It cost more than that and left 10.5%.
- The 30-name version did not dilute the edge. It was the best of the five on gains vs losses and on luck.

My opinion: Volatility-braking the overnight book is a dead end. The brake is the wrong tool for a book whose whole edge is in jumpy stocks. It sells exactly the jumpiness that pays. And the fold record (2 of 4, losing to SPY in 2009–2015) says even the unbraked edge may be fading as the data gets more complete. I would not spend another trial on brake targets here. If this family gets another try, the fix for the 1998 fall has to come from what is picked, not from how much is held: for example, drop the stocks whose overnight gain came from one or two huge gaps (likely one-off earnings jumps), and keep those that drifted up overnight steadily. That keeps the book's character and should make it calmer without paying to sit in cash. Before that, though, the lab should check how the unbraked overnight book did in 2009–2015. If it also lost to SPY there, drop the family.


### 2026-10-09

### 2026-10-09 -- Sera 20261009-2105: the hard gate refuses

`lab walkforward M0053`: 2 of 4 folds, 2009-2015 edge -3.8 points. `lab promote` would exit 2 on the folds condition, so no promotion was attempted. The brake bought the 20% limit at about four points of yearly return and lost the unbraked parent's fold record (3 of 4) and its positive recent-era edge (+1.1): the brake removed the part of the book that worked.
methods.verdict: The weekly brake fixed the fall but paid too much for it: 10.5-10.6% a year on your money with an 18.8-19.0% worst fall, against 15.1% unbraked, and it lost to SPY in 2009-2015, so the promotion gate would refuse it

methods.name: Drizzle picks without the cash periods: park in SPY instead of cash when the trend switch is off
methods.hypothesis: The drizzle blend (M0036-BLEND) and its braked twin (M0044) earn their whole edge in 2002-2008, when the SPY-200 trend switch held them in cash through the crash, and trail SPY by 4.8 to 7.1 points a year from 2009 to 2015. That says the stock picking itself may add nothing, and the switch's cash is doing the work. Test the picking alone: the same 20 drizzle-blend picks, monthly, fractional, at Gotrade's real fees, but with the trend switch off (variant ALWAYS-IN) and with the switch on but SPY as the parking spot instead of cash (variant PARK-SPY). Expected: ALWAYS-IN beats SPY over 2009-2015 only if continuity is a real stock-picking edge; if it trails there too, the drizzle signal is dead in this universe and the family should be closed. PARK-SPY should keep most of the 2009-2015 market return while losing some 2008 protection, so its worst fall will likely break 20%.

methods.name: Buy the dip inside the winners: last year's strongest stocks, entered after a bad month
methods.hypothesis: The bounce book showed a one-month fall is worth little as a stand-alone signal (about SPY's return, a 27% worst fall), but the classic 12-1 momentum skips the latest month precisely because recent losers bounce. Among the top 60 names by plain 12-1 total momentum (not residual, so the family is not the test-failed residual one), hold the 20 with the worst last-month return relative to the market, equal weight, SPY-200 gate, fractional at Gotrade's real fees on monthly-hold-frac-gotrade with the monthly top-up. Controls: the 20 with the best last month (the mirror), and plain top-20 momentum. Success means beating the plain momentum control on the worst fall at similar return, and winning a majority of walk-forward folds. Expected failure: the pullback pushes the book down into weaker momentum names and the 2009 junk rally still hits it, the same way it hit the parent.

methods.name: Steady overnight drift, not one big gap: overnight winners without the single-jump stocks
methods.hypothesis: M0050-TOT-ON earned 15.1% a year funded with a 22.8% worst fall and kept its edge out of sample (3 of 4 walk-forward folds, +1.1% vs SPY in 2009-2015); M0053 showed a volatility brake fixes the fall only by giving up 4.6 points of return and the fold record. Fix the fall through selection instead: among the 40 best 12-1 momentum names, rank on the overnight sum after removing each name's largest 3 (or 5) overnight gaps of the window, or on the share of positive overnight sessions, so the book holds names that drift up overnight steadily rather than ones carried by one or two earnings jumps that gap down together in a shock. Unbraked, monthly-hold-frac-gotrade, 20 and 30 names. Success: worst fall under 20% with funded return above 13.7% and a majority of folds kept.

insights.title: Volatility scaling buys drawdown at a near-linear price in return
insights.body: Scaling top-20 momentum to a 10-12% own-volatility target cut max DD from 22% to 11-13% but also CAGR from 16% to 6-7.6%, because a ~22%-vol book is held at about half exposure all the time, not just in crashes. The frontier passes near DD 13% at SPY's CAGR. To beat SPY under DD 15% we need more return per unit of risk, or de-risking that triggers only in dangerous regimes.

insights.title: Delisted stocks and fundamentals
insights.body: The store has no delisted names (survivorship makes stock results optimistic) and no fundamentals, so value, quality, profitability and earnings-surprise strategies, the best-documented factors after momentum, cannot be tested. A point-in-time source such as Sharadar or a CRSP/Compustat-like feed would unlock them and make every stock result more honest.

insights.title: The 15% max-DD bar over 1996-2015 includes two -50% crashes
insights.body: The dev window contains the 2000-02 and 2008-09 bear markets. Any strategy with meaningful equity exposure must sidestep most of both to stay under 15%, so the gate rewards crash avoidance above everything else. Expect winners to be regime-switching or heavily de-risked designs, and expect their test-window (2015-2026, one sharp 2020 crash) behaviour to differ.

insights.title: Weekly risk checks with monthly re-ranking
insights.body: M0001's weekly variant re-ranked and re-scaled together, which more than doubled turnover and cut PF to 1.49. A rule set that re-ranks monthly but re-scales exposure weekly would test whether faster risk control helps without the whipsaw cost. That needs a new TradeRules cadence split (rank cadence vs resize cadence).

insights.title: M0005 promoted to the paper roster as FND
insights.body:
Promoted to the paper roster as `FND`.

Variant: `M0005-ALL`. Roster object: `FUNDAMENTAL`. Frozen spec digest: `4a9dacc37478bf4d17b3ba35cbebd9e0c3f8759f122c4596f7cd9d076d8ef530`.

The roster row is `status='active'` with no `paper_start`: the next paper night freezes the spec and starts its own clock, so the paper record begins at the promotion and claims nothing earlier. `backtest.registry.REGISTRY` was not appended to -- a promoted method reaches the roster through the roster's own resolver, so the lab's multiple-testing count is unchanged by this.

insights.title: FND, a company-fundamentals picker, now trades on paper, and paper is its real test
insights.body:
Most strategies Sera has tried pick stocks by how their price has moved. This one is different: each month it picks the 20 big US companies whose own reports look best. It favours companies that are cheap next to what they own, earn well on their money, make healthy profits on what they sell, and recently beat what was expected of their earnings. Those four signals have a long track record in finance research.

**Why it went to paper even though the history test marked it "rejected".** The company reports Sera can read only start in 2015. The history test runs from 1996 to 2015, so for 19 of those 20 years the strategy had nothing to go on and just sat in cash. That's why it "failed": it never really got to play. The idea wasn't proven wrong. It was never tested.

Waiting is the only fair test left. From here on, FND trades every night with pretend money, its rules are locked, and nothing before its first night counts. That's also why it isn't a candidate for real money: it hasn't earned it yet.

**What to watch:** month by month, does it keep up with or beat SPY, and how far does it fall in a bad month? A few good months could be luck. A year of steady results would mean something.

insights.title: A slow signal does not get better by checking it more often
insights.body:
The lab has a stock picker that cuts its own exposure when the market gets choppy. It measures choppiness over the past three months. We wondered whether checking that measure weekly instead of monthly would catch crashes faster, so we built the ability to pick stocks on one schedule and set exposure on another, and tried every combination.

Checking weekly did not help. It made things slightly worse. The reason is simple once you see it: a three-month average barely moves in a week. Reading it every Monday gives back almost the same number it gave a month ago, so the faster schedule learns nothing new. What it does do is create four times as many chances to shuffle the book around that same unchanged number, and each shuffle costs a little. The worst fall improved by less than one point, from 11.0 percent to 10.3 percent, while yearly growth dropped from 6.1 percent to 4.8 percent. We paid more than we got.

The cleanest proof sits in the version with the market-trend filter switched off. Measured monthly and measured weekly, it scored identically. With nothing else in front of it, re-reading the choppiness number weekly changed literally nothing.

The useful lesson is a rule of thumb for everything the lab builds next. How often it is worth re-checking something is decided by how fast that something actually moves, not by how often we are willing to trade. Pair a three-month measure with a monthly schedule. If we want a genuinely faster reaction, we need a measure that genuinely moves faster, such as one built from the last few weeks rather than the last few months.

One thing did come out of it worth keeping. Splitting the two schedules let us settle an old question: the heavy trading in the weekly version came almost entirely from re-choosing which stocks to hold, not from adjusting how much to hold. Re-choosing costs about eight times as much trading as re-sizing. That is now a measured fact rather than a guess.

insights.title: Spreading money more cleverly is not the same as holding less of it
insights.body: We took the stock picker that buys the twenty strongest risers and, instead of splitting the money evenly between them, worked out from a year of daily prices which mix of those same twenty moves around the least, and bought that mix. It worked as mathematics and failed as safety. The month-to-month wobble of the account dropped by about a fifth. The worst fall, which is the thing the owner actually cares about and the thing our rules measure, dropped from 22.2% to 21.6% - almost nothing - while the yearly rate of return fell from 16.2% to 13.7%. We paid two and a half points of return for half a point of safety. The lesson is that wobble and worst fall are two different risks and a clever split only touches the first one. An ordinary month is made of twenty stocks disagreeing with each other, and a clever split smooths that out. A bad month is made of twenty stocks all falling together, and then there is no clever split, because they were all the same bet to begin with. The proof is the version we ran with the safety switch turned off: it fell 54% at its worst and lost 41% in 2008, slightly worse than just owning the market through the crash. The earlier method that simply held half its money in cash fell 18% in the same test. Holding less protects you. Holding the same amount, arranged more intelligently, does not. What to do about it: stop trying weighting schemes inside a single-theme book. Risk parity and its cousins would hit the same wall for the same reason. Safety in this kind of portfolio has to come from owning less of it at the right moments, or from owning something genuinely different, not from rearranging the same bet.

insights.title: The crash that keeps blocking us is 2006, and our safety switch never saw it
insights.body: Every version of the strongest-risers picker that uses the market safety switch - hold stocks while the market is above its 200-day average, otherwise sit in cash - has its worst moment in the same five months: March to August 2006. Not the dot-com bust, not 2008. In those five months the market itself fell at worst 7.6% and never once dipped below its 200-day average, so the safety switch stayed in the on position the entire time and the book rode it all the way down, losing about 18%. What crashed in 2006 was not the market. It was the theme: the energy, materials and emerging-market names that had all climbed smoothly for a year unwound together in May. This matters because it reframes the problem. We have been trying to make the book safer in general, when what actually blocks us is one specific kind of event that our one safety switch is blind to by construction - a crash in what we own while the market around it is fine. Worse, the clever-split experiment made 2006 worse rather than better, because the optimiser leans toward whatever has been calmest over the past year, and in 2006 the calmest names were exactly the smooth one-way climbers that broke hardest. A year of quiet upward drift looks like safety to the arithmetic and is in truth a crowded trade. What to do about it: give the book a second safety switch that watches the book itself rather than the market. When the account is more than some distance below its own previous high, cut back until it recovers. That is pointed straight at the event that keeps stopping us, and unlike holding permanent cash it costs nothing in the calm years. It is queued as the next trial.

insights.title: Taking the market's move out of a stock's score is the cheapest safety we have bought so far
insights.body:
Until now, every way we found to make the strategy fall less has cost about as much return as it saved. Shrinking positions when markets get jumpy cut the worst fall from 22% to 13%, and it cut the yearly return from 16% to 8% doing it - roughly one point of return for one point of safety.

The market-adjusted picker is the first exception. Before ranking stocks on how much they rose over the past year, it subtracts the part of each rise that the whole market explains, and ranks on what is left - the company's own story. It stays just as fully invested as before, buys the same number of names, and still turned a 22.2% worst fall into a 19.6% one while giving up only 1.2 points of yearly return. That is about half price.

Why it works: a stock that rose mostly because the market rose is a bet on the market, not on the company. A book full of those bets is a leveraged market bet in disguise, and it falls hardest exactly when the market turns. Removing that part of the score leaves a book of genuine company winners that does not all move together.

What to do about it: this is a better starting point, not a finished strategy, because 19.6% is still well over the 15% limit. The right next move is to put our existing position-shrinking overlay on top of this better book rather than on the old one - we would be spending a 15% yearly return down to about 11% instead of spending a 16% one down to 8%. That is the first combination where the arithmetic reaches the limit with something left over for the owner.

insights.title: A buy-only strategy's crash is the market's crash, so a cleverer stock score cannot prevent it
insights.body:
The research papers behind this experiment report that market-adjusted momentum largely cures the sudden collapses that plague momentum strategies. We tested that claim directly by removing our market-trend safety switch and letting the stock score fend for itself. It fell 51% from its peak and lost 34% in 2008 - no better than the plain version.

The reason is a mismatch we should remember. Those papers study a portfolio that buys winners and sells losers short at the same time. Its collapses really are a momentum-specific event: after a bad market the losers it is short are the jumpy, high-market-sensitivity names, and when the market rebounds those explode upward and the short side blows up. We never sell short. We only buy. So our collapses are simply the market's collapses, arriving through the stocks we hold, and no improvement to how we choose stocks can remove them.

What to do about it: keep treating the market-trend switch - being in cash when the market is below its long-term average - as the one thing that controls our worst falls, and treat every stock-scoring idea as a way to earn more while invested, never as a substitute for it. Also, when a paper promises crash protection, check first whether it is protecting the short side we do not have. Usefully, the test also showed where our remaining risk actually sits: with the switch on, 2001, 2002 and 2008 were all flat, and the deepest fall of the whole twenty years came from one fast shock in the autumn of 1998 that the switch reacted to too late.

insights.title: The falls that hurt this strategy happen in calm markets, not crashes
insights.body:
A momentum strategy that buys the twenty strongest stocks and sits in cash when the market is below its 200-day average has almost no bad years. Over 1996-2015 its worst calendar year was about minus three percent, and 2001, 2002 and 2008 came out flat, because it was in cash through those crashes.

Its losses come from somewhere else entirely. The four worst spells were March to August 2006, the summer of 1998, the spring of 2010 and the autumn of 2011. In every one of them the market was fine and the particular stocks the strategy had crowded into reversed. Spring 2006 is the clearest: commodity and emerging-market names had run hard, the market stayed comfortably above its 200-day average so the cash switch never tripped, and the holdings unwound anyway.

This matters because the usual safety device is a brake tied to how much the holdings have been bouncing around lately. That brake cannot help here. The jump in bounciness and the loss are the same event, and a three-month measurement needs weeks to notice it, so the brake comes on after the money is gone. It protected against long bad stretches, which is real, and did nothing about sharp ones.

What to do about it: stop trying to predict these falls from past bounciness and react to the fall itself. A brake that watches whether the stocks currently held are below their own recent high can move on day one of a reversal instead of six weeks in. That is the next thing worth testing.

insights.title: Turning a strategy down is not the same as making it safer, and the lab keeps proving it
insights.body:
The lab has now run three versions of the same experiment: take the strongest stock picker it has, and shrink how much money it puts to work when things look risky. The unshrunk picker grew 16.2 percent a year and fell 22.2 percent at its worst. Shrinking it all the time gave 7.6 percent and 12.9 percent. Shrinking it only when the holdings were unusually jumpy gave 12.6 percent and 18.4 percent.

Line those up against how much money each one actually kept in stocks on an average day, and the picture is stark. Every single version gave up roughly the same amount of fall for each unit of money it put at work: around thirty-five, in those units, whether it braked hard, softly, cleverly, or not at all. The brake was not removing risk. It was turning the whole thing down, and return and risk came down together in step.

The one real gain is smaller and worth keeping: braking only when the holdings are jumpy for themselves earns more per unit of money at work than braking all the time, about 24 against 21 in the same units. A well-aimed brake is better than a permanent one. It is just a refinement on a dial, not an escape from it.

The risk this creates for the lab is spending run after run on that dial. Because the trade is so close to a straight line, where any setting lands can now be read off in advance, and the honest answer is that no setting of it produces a strategy that is better rather than smaller. The remaining problem is the quality of the stock picking itself, not what is done with the picks afterwards.

insights.title: The lab's own searching is raising the bar it has to clear
insights.body:
Before any strategy is allowed near real money, the lab asks how likely its result is to be genuine rather than the best of many lucky tries. The more things have been tried, the better a result has to be. That count has now reached eighty-five, and the bar has moved with it.

Working from where this run landed, a strategy of this shape now needs a reward-per-unit-of-wobble score of about one a year to clear the bar. The best this lab has ever recorded is 0.89, from the plain momentum picker with no brake on it. This run's best was 0.87. Everything tried so far sits just under the line, and roughly every seventy further trials pushes the line a little further away.

The important part is where that score does not come from. Across this whole family of experiments the score barely moved: 0.89 with no brake, 0.81 braked all the time, 0.87 braked only in jumpy spells. Adjusting how much money is at work changes the return and the swings together and leaves their ratio alone. So no amount of further work on brakes, targets or triggers will clear this bar.

What will clear it is picking better stocks: a signal that earns more for the risk it takes. That points the next runs at the queued work on momentum measured against what the market did anyway, and on weighting holdings by how they move together rather than equally. It also argues for being sparing with trials, because every one spent raises the bar for the ones after it.

insights.title: Sera 20261006-1137: three ways to make a winner safe, and only changing what we buy worked
insights.body:
Three sessions ran side by side, each trying a different way to make the same winning
strategy safe enough to use. The strategy is the one that keeps coming back: buy the twenty
stocks that rose most over the past year, refresh the list monthly, and sit in cash whenever
the market itself is below its long-run average. It makes about 16% a year against the
market's 8%. It has one flaw, and the whole lab is now organised around that flaw: at its
worst it fell 22% from a peak, and our limit is 15%.

There are only three places you can intervene. You can change how much you hold and when
(braking). You can change how the money is split between the names you hold (weighting). Or
you can change which names you pick in the first place (the score). This batch tried one of
each, deliberately, so that a failure would tell us something a success could not.

**Braking and weighting both failed, and failed for the same reason.** The first session
braked only when the basket itself turned jumpy, leaving it fully invested in calm spells.
The second kept the same twenty names and the same full investment, but worked out from the
past year of prices which mix of them moves together least, and held that mix instead of
equal amounts. Both beat the market comfortably. Neither got the worst fall below 17%.

The second session produced the cleanest evidence of the batch. Its clever splitting did
exactly what it promised: the day-to-day wobble dropped by almost a fifth, with every penny
